source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Founding claim as summarised by Elstein: hard diagnostic problems are solved by generating a few hypotheses early and using them to guide data collection. Each hypothesis predicts findings that should be present.
numbers: Source of the claim is Elstein, Shulman, Sprafka (1978); the book itself was not opened. No numbers in the review.
quote: Solutions to difficult diagnostic problems were found by generating a limited number of hypotheses early in the diagnostic process
limits: Review by the original author, 24 years later; it also restates the model as a guided search for these findings.
agent_relevance: S3 generate a few candidates early; S4 test by predicting what else must be true.

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Experienced physicians form hypotheses and a diagnostic plan quickly, and the quality of their hypotheses is higher than novices. Novices struggle to make a plan and some cannot move from collecting data to weighing possibilities.
numbers: No counts given in this review.
limits: Qualitative. Supports better hypotheses, not more.
agent_relevance: Quality of the candidate set matters more than its size; do not reward the agent for listing many.

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Content specificity challenges the model. Both successful and unsuccessful diagnosticians use hypothesis testing, so accuracy depends more on mastery of content than on strategy.
numbers: Review statement; cites Patel & Groen 1986 and Elstein 1978. No effect sizes.
limits: Expertise cannot be separated from content in practice, only analytically.
agent_relevance: A generic hypothesise-and-test scaffold will not substitute for domain knowledge. Gains must come from knowledge retrieval, not from the loop itself.

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Experts in familiar cases often do not test hypotheses explicitly. Experienced doctors probably use hypothetico-deductive reasoning only for difficult cases; easy cases are pattern recognition or direct retrieval.
numbers: Review statement citing Schmidt, Norman, Boshuizen 1990; Brooks, Norman, Allen 1991; Norman et al 1992.
quote: Easy cases can be solved by pattern recognition: difficult cases need systematic generation and testing of hypotheses.
limits: Difficulty is defined by the clinician's knowledge, so the same case can be easy or hard.
agent_relevance: Run the hypothesise-and-test loop only when a fast first answer fails a check (fits guardrail G1: doubt only on a signal).

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Errors seen from the problem-solving view: failure to generate the correct hypothesis, misreading evidence (especially visual cues), and misinterpreting evidence. In many hard cases the right answer is not in the initial set. Clinicians commit to a hypothesis early and find it hard to restructure.
numbers: Qualitative; cites Kassirer & Kopelman 1991 and Bordage 1999.
limits: Prevalence of these errors is stated as not established.
agent_relevance: Early hypotheses create anchoring risk. The agent needs a trigger to re-open the candidate set when checks fail (S3 re-entry).

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Decision-making view: diagnosis is opinion revision, with Bayes' theorem as the rule. Observed deviations: anchoring and insufficient adjustment, conservatism, order effects (later information weighs more), overemphasis of positive findings, discounting negative findings, reading findings as fitting a single hypothesis.
numbers: Narrative review; no pooled effect sizes. Authors say error prevalence is unknown and expert reasoning is likely right in most cases.
limits: The authors stress that both traditions study mistakes more than successes.
agent_relevance: Counting and updating belief should be done by code, not by the model's feel (G5).

source: Elstein & Schwarz (2002) Clinical problem solving and diagnostic decision making: selective review of the cognitive literature
finding: Educational consequence: problem-based learning was built to put hypothesis formulation and testing into early training. Case specificity showed the limits of teaching a general strategy, so the rationale moved to building a functional organisation of content (schemas).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Links the model to curriculum, not to measured error reduction.
agent_relevance: Same lesson for the agent: supply structure of knowledge, not only a procedure.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Background claim: the cognitive tradition began with Elstein, Shulman, Sprafka (1978) and held that diagnosticians reason like scientists. This was challenged by Groen & Patel (1985): the work seemed to present hypothetico-deductive reasoning as psychologically real rather than an intellectual tool. The authors say people may still use it where it is required.
numbers: Historical framing inside a 1991 conference paper.
limits: Written by a group that is itself a critic (McGill).
agent_relevance: The model is better read as a tool a reasoner can call on than as a description of every step.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Design: second, third and fourth year McGill medical students (4 per group) plus one cardiology resident. Two real cardiology cases split into three segments (complaint, past history, physical exam). Think-aloud, tentative diagnosis after each segment, 90-minute individual session.
numbers: N = 13 (12 students + 1 resident). Cases built so the first segment suggests one hypothesis and later segments contradict it.
limits: Very small sample; one specialty.
agent_relevance: Tests what happens to an early hypothesis when contradicting data arrive, the S3 to S4 hand-off.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Number of hypotheses generated at the first segment rose with training: second year mean 1.5, third year mean 3, fourth year mean 3.4, resident 5 in both cases. All subjects generated the initially suggested hypothesis.
numbers: 4 per student group, 1 resident.
limits: Counts hypotheses generated, not their quality. Goes against a simple reading of experts do not generate more, in this small sample.
agent_relevance: Breadth of the initial set can grow with knowledge; the claim only better, not more is not fully supported here.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Accuracy was low. Five of 13 reached the correct diagnosis: two second-year students, two fourth-year students and the resident. No third-year student was correct. Only the resident was correct on both cases. All subjects selected the important cues.
numbers: N = 13; two cases.
limits: Non-monotonic across years; small cells.
agent_relevance: More training did not guarantee better diagnoses; spotting the cues was not enough to reach the diagnosis.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Evaluation was mostly confirmation. Share of cues used as confirming relations: second year 71%, third and fourth year 88%, resident 92%. All second-year students kept the initial hypothesis despite contradictory data, ignoring the data or bending the hypothesis to fit. Third and fourth year students held concurrent hypotheses for different cue sets. The resident started with several hypotheses then narrowed to one that covered most data.
numbers: 4 per group, one resident; protocols coded as propositions and semantic networks (Patel & Groen 1986 method).
limits: Coding by the authors; no inter-rater figure seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence of confirmation bias in early-hypothesis testing; a disconfirm step must be forced by code.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Most inferences were forward (cue suggests hypothesis); all subjects mixed forward and backward reasoning. More forward-directed reasoning went with higher accuracy. The resident used backward inference to reach the solution of case 1 when given contradictory evidence.
numbers: 4 subjects used forward inference to conclude the final correct diagnosis, all in case 2.
limits: The paper's literature review says backward (hypothesis-to-data) reasoning is slow, loads working memory and is tied to unsuccessful performance.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-driven search is a fallback when direct data-to-diagnosis mapping fails, not the default expert mode.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Cited prior work (Joseph & Patel 1990, endocrinology): hypothesis generation did not separate low-knowledge from high-knowledge physicians; hypothesis evaluation did. High-knowledge subjects searched for confirmation and refined the first hypothesis. Low-knowledge subjects produced alternatives after already producing the correct one.
numbers: Secondhand description inside Arocha & Patel; Joseph & Patel not opened.
limits: Secondary report.
agent_relevance: Supports a two-stage view: generation draws on general knowledge, evaluation on specific knowledge.

source: Arocha & Patel (1991) Hypothesis generation and the coordination of theory and evidence in medical diagnostic reasoning
finding: Cited prior work (Patel, Groen, Norman, in press): students from a problem-based curriculum, trained in hypothetico-deductive diagnosis, used more backward reasoning and more elaboration. Conventional-curriculum students used more forward reasoning.
numbers: Secondhand; two studies by the original authors, not opened.
limits: Direction of effect on accuracy is not stated in the passage read.
agent_relevance: Training a hypothesis-first procedure can change reasoning direction without improving it; test any such scaffold against a plain baseline (G7).

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Design: 15 volunteers (5 endocrinologists, 5 third-year residents, 5 final-year students) each took a 15-minute history from one simulated outpatient with hypokalemic periodic paralysis linked to thyrotoxicosis. Accuracy needed both components named in the differential. Sixteen findings were marked relevant by an expert reference model.
numbers: N = 15; one case; videotaped, transcribed, coded for observations, findings, facets.
limits: One case, one specialty.
agent_relevance: Looks at data gathering during the interview, the S4 test side of the loop.

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Accuracy: 4 of 5 experts named both components (the fifth named the thyroid problem only). One resident named both; two named hyperthyroidism only; one saw periodic paralysis but not hypokalemia; one named neither. No student got the full diagnosis, though three saw the thyroid aspect.
numbers: 5 per group.
limits: Tiny groups.
agent_relevance: Domain knowledge decided who reached the full answer.

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Experts asked the fewest questions. Multivariate test on exchanges, observations, findings: group effect F(2,12) = 4.64, p < .05. Efficiency (findings per exchange) also differed by group: F(2,12) = 8.69, p < .01. Experts got comparable numbers of positive findings (14.4) to residents (14.6) and more than students (13) with fewer questions.
numbers: N = 15; exploratory ANOVAs without correction.
limits: Exploratory analyses; table values are partly garbled in the PDF text, so only the quoted statistics are recorded.
agent_relevance: Better hypotheses mean fewer, sharper questions; measure information gain per query, not number of queries.

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Experts obtained 72% of the 16 relevant findings, residents 60%, students 45% (F(2,12) = 4.46, p < .05). Of all findings each group elicited, 50% were relevant for experts, 33% for residents, 31% for students.
limits: Relevance set by one expert reference model.
agent_relevance: Selectivity of the question set, not its size, separated experts.

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Positive findings per question-answer exchange: experts 18.6, residents 12.2, students 10.6 (F(2,12) = 7.28, p < .01). Authors read this as experts recognising the problem early and pursuing hypotheses that predict candidate findings. Residents elicited almost as many negative as positive findings, read as difficulty building one coherent representation and a wish to rule out many alternatives.
limits: Interpretation is the authors', not tested by manipulation.
agent_relevance: Weak solvers spread tests across many hypotheses; strong solvers test the hypothesis that predicts specific findings.

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Authors' summary of the founding work: Elstein et al. (1978) and Barrows et al. (1978) studied process, not content. Their findings did not separate student from expert physician except in the accuracy of the diagnostic hypotheses.
numbers: Statement in the introduction, not a new measurement.
quote: Their findings did not discriminate between between student and expert physician except for the accuracy of diagnostic hypotheses.
limits: Written by critics of the process-only approach.
agent_relevance: Core reason the model was dropped as the explanation of expertise.

source: Kaufman & Patel (1988) The nature of expertise in the clinical interview: interactive medical problem solving
finding: Secondhand: Kassirer & Gorry (1978) found that diagnoses are most often made during history-taking. Patel & Groen (1986) found accurate experts reasoned forward from text to diagnosis; experts who misdiagnosed reasoned backward, posting a cause and then collecting confirming evidence.
numbers: Kassirer & Gorry 1978 and Patel & Groen 1986 not opened; known only through this paper's introduction.
limits: Secondary report.
agent_relevance: Backward hypothesis-first reasoning that only collects confirming evidence is the failure mode to guard against.

source: Sprafka (1973) doctoral dissertation, Michigan State (via a search-result summary)
finding: Reported only in a search-result summary: 30 fourth-year students were told to generate many or few hypotheses, early or late. Instructions about hypothesis generation had no effect on outcome.
numbers: N = 30 as summarised. Full text could not be opened (repository access limited).
limits: Secondhand and unverified; treat as a lead to check.
agent_relevance: If true, telling a reasoner to generate more hypotheses or to generate them earlier does not help. Consistent with the Monteiro and Norman finding in the SUBFIELDS note.

source: Style (1979) Intuition and problem solving, J R Coll Gen Pract 29:71-74
finding: A general-practice essay stating that GPs form initial hypotheses in the first few minutes of a consultation, then search to define them, and that hypotheses are redefined many times. It ties the first step to intuition and probable pattern recognition and cites Elstein et al. 1972 and Leaper et al. 1973.
numbers: No data, no counts. Essay.
quote: In the first few minutes of their consultations physicians form initial hypotheses about their patients' problems.
limits: Weak evidence; shows how fast the model spread into primary care teaching.
agent_relevance: Early hypothesis formation is fast and intuitive, so S3 generation should be cheap and S4 testing the costly step.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: Design: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on free-response MedQA USMLE Step 2/3 diagnosis questions (95 train, 518 test). Five few-shot prompts with two worked examples each: plain chain of thought, differential-diagnosis CoT, intuitive, analytic, Bayesian. Two blinded physicians graded each answer; McNemar test against plain CoT.
numbers: Test set 518 (497 for GPT-4 after 21 API errors). Kappa 0.93 (GPT-3.5) and 0.98 (GPT-4).
limits: Prompts were few-shot with only two examples; one dataset; graded by the authors.
agent_relevance: Direct test of a form a differential first prompt, which is the hypothetico-deductive opening move.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: GPT-3.5: plain CoT 46%; intuitive 48% (P = 0.9); differential-diagnosis CoT 38% (difference -8%, P < 0.001); analytic 40% (-6%, P = 0.001); Bayesian 42% (-4%, P = 0.02). Forming a differential hurt the weaker model.
numbers: Test N = 518; self-consistency applied to GPT-3.5 CoT prompts.
limits: Single prompt set; older model.
agent_relevance: A hypothesis-first prompt can reduce accuracy in a weaker model. Must be tested per model (G7).

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: GPT-4: plain CoT 76%; intuitive 77% (+0.8%, P = 0.73); differential diagnosis 78% (+2.2%, CI -1.4 to +5.8, P = 0.24); analytic 78% (+1.6%, P = 0.35); Bayesian 72% (-3.4%, P = 0.07). No prompt beat plain CoT by a significant margin.
numbers: Test N = 497.
limits: The differential gain of 2.2 points is not significant.
agent_relevance: Forming a differential costs nothing in GPT-4 but gives no measured accuracy gain; its value is the readable rationale.

source: Savage et al. (2023) Diagnostic reasoning prompts reveal the potential for LLM interpretability in medicine
finding: Prompt development lesson: prompts that encouraged step-by-step reasoning without fixing the steps did better, and a prompt focused on one reasoning strategy beat one that mixed several.
numbers: Observed on the 95-question training set with GPT-3.5.
limits: Informal development finding, no statistics given.
agent_relevance: Do not stack several clinical reasoning styles in one prompt.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models
finding: Sequential Diagnosis Benchmark: 304 NEJM clinicopathological cases turned into stepwise encounters. The agent starts from a short abstract and asks a gatekeeper model for findings and tests. Scored on accuracy and cost. Generalist physicians (US/UK, median 12 years) reached 20% at $2,963 per case. GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745. o3 78.6% at $7,850.
numbers: N = 304 cases; physician cohort size not read.
limits: Judge is o3 with a rubric; cut-off score 4 of 5; cases are published (leak risk).
agent_relevance: First large test of the full loop: hypotheses, then chosen tests, then revision.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models
finding: MAI-DxO is a model-agnostic orchestrator with five roles: Dr Hypothesis (probability-ranked differential, top 3, Bayesian updates), Dr Test-Chooser (up to 3 tests that best split leading hypotheses), Dr Challenger (devil's advocate against anchoring), Dr Stewardship (cost), Dr Checklist. A chain of debate ends in a question, a test or a diagnosis.
numbers: Design description.
quote: Dr. Hypothesis Maintains a probability-ranked differential diagnosis with the top three most likely conditions
limits: Cost of roles is folded into the benchmark cost.
agent_relevance: Closest published implementation of S3 generate and S4 test as separate fixed roles.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models
finding: Results: MAI-DxO with o3 got 79.9% at $2,397, or 85.5% at $7,184 in the maximum-accuracy ensemble, against o3 alone 78.6% at $7,850. The orchestrator raised accuracy of models from several providers by an average of 11 points. Cost fell by more than half versus off-the-shelf models at similar accuracy.
numbers: N = 304; costs are model-estimated prices.
limits: The accuracy gain over o3 is 1.3 points at the cheap setting; most of the win is cost. Gain over weaker models is larger. Ablation of single roles was not read.
agent_relevance: The scaffold paid for itself mainly through cheaper test choice, not a big accuracy jump on the strongest model.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models
finding: Authors' case analysis: where MAI-DxO disagreed with the o3 baseline, it often sought disconfirming evidence and changed path, which they credit to explicit hypothesis tracking and the Challenger role. The baseline seemed to anchor on first impressions and lacked a sense of the value of information.
numbers: Qualitative observation, no counts read.
limits: Not an ablation; roles were not removed one by one in the part read.
agent_relevance: Explicit candidate tracking plus a forced disconfirmation step is the proposed working mechanism.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: o1-preview on 143 NEJM clinicopathological cases: the correct diagnosis was in its differential in 78.3% (95% CI 70.7 to 84.8) and was the first suggestion in 52% (CI 44 to 61). Pre-cutoff 79.8% vs post-cutoff 73.5% (p = 0.59), so no clear contamination effect.
numbers: N = 143; two physician raters agreed on 120/143 (84%, kappa 0.66).
limits: Published cases; no real-time workflow.
agent_relevance: An LLM's differential catches the answer much more often than its first guess. Candidate sets pay when a selector exists.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: On 70 cases used earlier for GPT-4, o1-preview gave an exact or very close diagnosis in 88.6% vs 72.9% for GPT-4 (p = .015). It chose the correct next test in 87.5% of 132 cases, a helpful test in another 11%, and an unhelpful one in 1.5%.
numbers: McNemar test; historical GPT-4 control from a different study.
limits: Historical control, not same-time comparison.
agent_relevance: Test selection from a differential is already strong in reasoning models.

source: Brodeur et al. (2024) Superhuman performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician
finding: NEJM Healer reasoning documentation (problem representation, prioritised differential, justification): o1-preview got a perfect R-IDEA score in 78 of 80 responses, GPT-4 in 47/80, attendings 28/80, residents 16/80 (all p < 0.0001). Share of cannot-miss diagnoses in the triage differential: median 0.92 for o1-preview, not significantly above GPT-4, attendings or residents.
numbers: 20 cases x 4 sections = 80 responses; historical human controls.
limits: R-IDEA grades the writing of the reasoning, not whether it caused a right answer. Cannot-miss recall was not better.
agent_relevance: A good-looking hypothesis list is easy for models; do not mistake it for better diagnosis.

source: McDuff et al. (2023) Towards accurate differential diagnosis with large language models
finding: 20 clinicians reviewed 302 NEJM cases. The LLM alone listed the right diagnosis in its top 10 in 59.1% vs 33.6% for unassisted clinicians (p = 0.04). Assisted clinicians reached 51.7% with the LLM, 44.4% with search, and 36.1% with no assistance (LLM vs none p < 0.01; LLM vs search p = 0.03).
numbers: N = 302 cases, 20 clinicians, randomised to two assist arms; baseline unassisted differential taken first.
limits: Top-10 list accuracy, not final diagnosis; clinicians may be less careful than in practice.
agent_relevance: Machine-generated candidate lists widen human hypothesis sets, which supports using a model at S3.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing diagnostic accuracy through multi-agent conversations: LLMs to mitigate cognitive bias
finding: Sixteen published case reports of misdiagnosis driven by cognitive bias, 80 GPT-4 simulations with four agents (final diagnoser, devil's advocate against anchoring and confirmation, facilitator against premature closure, recorder). Initial diagnosis accuracy was 0/80; after discussion the top differential was right in 71.3% (57/80) and the final two in 80.0% (64/80).
numbers: 80 simulations on 16 cases (5 per case); no plain-model re-prompt control read.
limits: The initial diagnosis was set by case selection (all cases were misdiagnosed), so 0% is by design. No control for simply asking the model again.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a forced devil's-advocate step can reopen a wrong early hypothesis; control missing (G7).

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Quantifying the reasoning abilities of LLMs on real-world clinical cases (MedR-Bench)
finding: MedR-Bench, 1,453 case reports. DeepSeek-R1 diagnosis accuracy was 71.79% after one round of examination recommendation, 76.18% after free multi-turn information gathering, and 89.76% when given all examination results (oracle). OpenAI-o3-mini went 64.99% to 67.19% from one-turn to free-turn. Reasoning factuality over 90% but key steps often missed.
numbers: Five reasoning LLMs; patient simulated by an LLM agent; automated reasoning evaluator.
limits: Case reports are published text; simulated patient may leak answers.
agent_relevance: Most of the loss is in choosing what to ask, not in interpreting results once seen; the S4 test-choice step is the weak point.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments
finding: With bias prompts GPT-4 unbiased accuracy was 52%. Patient cognitive bias cut it to 48% (normalised 92%); doctor cognitive bias to 50.3% (96.7%); implicit bias in patient to 51.3% and in doctor to 50.5%. Mixtral-8x7B baseline was 37%.
numbers: Bias injected by prompting simulated agents; sample size not read in the part examined.
limits: Effects are small in absolute terms (about 2 to 4 points); statistical tests not read.
agent_relevance: Small measured harm from induced bias in the simulated setting; do not over-invest in bias patches.
